lists.text:
1. Launch a citywide campaign teaching residents how to plan meals, store food properly, and use leftovers.
2. Offer discounted home compost bins and training to households with outdoor space.
3. Provide curbside food-scrap collection for residents who cannot compost at home.
4. Require large food businesses to separate edible surplus for donation before discarding it.
5. Create a centralized platform that matches surplus food from businesses with local hunger-relief organizations.
6. Fund refrigerated vans to transport donated perishables safely across the city.
7. Install community refrigerators in accessible locations with clear food-safety rules and maintenance plans.
8. Help restaurants measure kitchen waste and identify their biggest opportunities for prevention.
9. Encourage restaurants to offer smaller portions at proportionally lower prices.
10. Make take-home containers readily available to restaurant customers.
11. Support apps that let bakeries, cafés, and grocers sell surplus food at discounted prices before closing.
12. Partner with supermarkets to create clearly marked sections for discounted near-date products.
13. Promote consumer education explaining the difference between food quality dates and safety guidance.
14. Organize volunteers to glean unharvested produce from farms near the city.
15. Coordinate neighborhood fruit-tree harvesting teams to collect produce that owners cannot use.
16. Establish a municipal purchasing policy that accepts cosmetically imperfect produce.
17. Help schools schedule lunch periods long enough for students to finish their meals.
18. Introduce school cafeteria share tables for eligible unopened food under local health rules.
19. Use student taste tests to improve school menus before purchasing ingredients in bulk.
20. Train cafeteria staff to prepare food in smaller batches based on real-time demand.
21. Offer grants for food businesses to upgrade refrigeration and temperature monitoring.
22. Create a rapid-response network to rescue food during power outages and equipment failures.
23. Ask event organizers to submit surplus-food recovery plans when applying for city permits.
24. Connect caterers with donation partners before weddings, conferences, and festivals.
25. Encourage buffet operators to use smaller serving trays and replenish them more frequently.
26. Provide residents with practical guidance on freezing surplus ingredients and prepared meals.
27. Host cooking classes focused on using commonly discarded edible parts such as stems and greens.
28. Establish a commercial kitchen where entrepreneurs can turn surplus ingredients into marketable products.
29. Partner with breweries and bakeries to develop food products from suitable grain and bread byproducts.
30. Help food manufacturers improve inventory forecasting using shared technical assistance.
31. Encourage grocery stores to sell loose produce so shoppers can buy only the quantities they need.
32. Work with retailers to replace perishable-food multibuy promotions with equivalent single-item discounts.
33. Offer smaller food packages at fair unit prices through partnerships with local retailers.
34. Organize neighborhood food swaps for unopened pantry items and surplus garden produce.
35. Install pantry shelves in apartment buildings for residents to share eligible shelf-stable foods.
36. Provide multilingual food-storage guides through libraries, clinics, and community centers.
37. Create a voluntary city certification recognizing businesses that demonstrate measurable food-waste reductions.
38. Publish annual citywide food-waste data to track progress and target underperforming sectors.
39. Conduct waste audits in municipal buildings and adjust food purchasing based on the findings.
40. Require city-funded meal programs to forecast attendance and record unserved portions.
41. Help hospitals and care homes offer meal ordering closer to service time to reduce unwanted trays.
42. Develop emergency donation procedures for school closures and canceled public events.
43. Provide small grants to food pantries for shelving, refrigeration, and inventory systems.
44. Extend food-pantry pickup hours so working residents can collect perishables before they spoil.
45. Use community surveys to align donated food with recipients’ dietary needs and cooking facilities.
46. Establish safe, regulated pathways for suitable food scraps to become animal feed.
47. Send unavoidable food waste to anaerobic digestion facilities where feasible.
48. Offer technical support to apartment managers for shared food-scrap collection areas.
49. Run a household food-waste challenge that rewards participants for reducing measured edible waste.
50. Convene a city food-waste task force to coordinate agencies, businesses, nonprofits, and residents around measurable reduction targets.
